# Kuṇālajātaka (Ja 536)
**ID:** Ja 536
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kuṇālajātaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja536
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kuṇālajātaka* (Ja 536) is framed around a story told by the Buddha while staying beside Lake Kuṇāla to five hundred monks who were afflicted with discontent [SuttaCentral]. It occupies an exceptional position within the Pali Jātaka collection because it is the only Jātaka to preserve canonical prose alongside verse, as attested by the presence of a dedicated word commentary explaining both its prose and verse portions [Kingsbury 2002; Norman 1983; Appleton 2010]. This canonical prose consists of narrative sections and elaborate descriptive passages marked by unusually long compound words depicting the sylvan beauty of the Himavat mountains [Collins 1998; Norman 1983], much of it composed in an archaic rhythmical style identified as *vedha* [Norman 2006]. The canonical prose begins with the pratīka *evam akkhāyati* [Norman 1983].
Substantively, the text comprises an atypical cycle of sub-stories and verses that dwell on the wickedness, treachery, and fickleness of women [Norman 1983; Harvey 2000; Shyu 2008]. Scholars observe that many of these verses represent pan-Indian secular misogynous gnomic literature rather than specifically Buddhist teachings [Norman 1983; Harvey 2000]. In contrast to the Pali version's pervasive ascetic misogyny, the parallel narrative preserved as story 62 in the Chinese *Liu du ji jing*, as well as a later thirteenth-century Sinhalese derivative, lacks misogynous tendencies entirely [Harvey 2000; Shyu 2008]. Text-critical analysis suggests that individual stanzas, such as the unique śloka *sabbā nadī…* among a run of triṣṭubh verses, represent early interpolations [von Hinüber 1994], while thematic parallels have been noted with the Sanskrit *Avimāraka* drama [Nakamura 1980]. A major critical edition and study utilizing manuscript evidence from the commentary and sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) was published by W. B. Bollée in 1970 [Norman 1983; Appleton 2010; von Hinüber 1994].
In terms of parallels and text reuse, SuttaCentral records passage-level links with the *Kaṇḍarījātaka* (Ja 341), the *Cūḷakuṇālajātaka* (Ja 464), and the *Asātamantajātaka* (Ja 61), while noting its citation in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.4.8) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus substantiates this extensive intra-Pali reuse, registering near-identical passages in Ja 464 (§63.4–75.4 matching §1.1–12.4 with 1.0 similarity) and Ja 341 (§59.4–63.4 matching §1.1–4.4 with 0.98 similarity), alongside massive overlap with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and shared segments with the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2) and *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments are also registered by DharmaNexus with Tibetan texts including the *Jinamārgāvatāra* (D3964) and *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155), as well as Chinese canonical collections [DharmaNexus].
